hints.hint:
A number N is shown but nobody is told whether it is the sum or the product: both readings stay live for everyone at once. First move: for a holder of x, write the partner set C(x) = {N-x, N/x}, keeping only natural values (N/x only when x divides N). "I don't know" means |C(x)| >= 2.

Trap: do not case-split into "it must be the sum" / "it must be the product". You will contradict both, then guess. A contradiction means you wrongly assumed the reading was known; reinstate both, do not restart.

Filter in speaking order: list D, the first speaker's surviving values (divisors of N are few, so D is short). The next speaker is ignorant iff two or more elements of C(y) lie in D. Sweep once and box the unique survivor.

hints.hint: For "all roots lie on one circle" problems, take moduli before hunting roots. From (z-a)^n = c(z-b)^n get |z-a| = k|z-b| with k = |c|^(1/n). TRAP: |c|*|z-b|^n means c is NOT raised to the n-th power; compute k as a plain number and check k^n = |c| before continuing, since a wrong k gives a wrong but perfectly self-consistent circle. Then set z = x+iy, square, collect the x^2+y^2 terms, divide by their coefficient, complete the square, read off center and radius (an Apollonius circle; k=1 degenerates to a line). Verify against the ORIGINAL equation, never your derived one: solve (z-a)/(z-b) = k for its real root and check its distance to your center equals your radius. Then box.

hints.hint: Union = sum of areas minus overlap, so maximize by minimizing overlap. Do this first, then never redo it: put the pinned corner at the origin, keep the small square axis-aligned, and let a single angle theta rotate the other shape. Prune before computing: only the two edges meeting at the pinned point can cut the small square, so ignore the far edges. Pick one convenient theta, find where those two rays exit the square, list the region's vertices in cyclic order, and shoelace. Repeat at one other theta. If the two values agree, that IS the answer: do not scan more angles, do not restart, do not re-verify. Box it immediately and keep the final write-up to three lines.

hints.hint:
Several hidden degree-n polynomials must jointly hit prescribed values at consecutive integers. Rewrite the target as a function of the INPUT x, not the position: an arithmetic progression over consecutive inputs is affine, L(x)=px+q.

First move: fix a polynomial P and set g=P-L. Subtracting an affine L leaves P's leading term untouched, so deg g = deg P exactly, NOT one less; getting that degree wrong is the main way this problem is lost. Each input handled by P is a root of g, so P serves at most deg P inputs; multiply by the number of polynomials.

A polynomial may be reused, so never conclude one input each. Check the cap is attained by giving each polynomial its own block of consecutive inputs where it interpolates L. When cap and construction agree, box the integer immediately; do not restart.

The incumbent named the g=P-L move but never pinned the degree, so I state deg g = deg P exactly as the headline trap, keep the reuse warning, and add an explicit commit-and-box rule to stop the looping rollout.

hints.hint:
Reduce to ONE unknown: put the free vertex at (t, g(t)) and its partner at (t+u, g(t)+v) for the given displacement (u,v), then solve g(t+u) = g(t) + v.

For y = log_c(ratio), adding v to the log multiplies the ratio by c^v in the GIVEN base c (c<1 shrinks it). Compute c^v as a number, then cross-multiply; using c^(-v) is the dominant error.

If the discriminant comes out negative, do NOT recheck earlier lines or restart with renamed variables: negate (u,v), shifting the other vertex, and redo only the cross-multiplication. Allow one flip, then commit.

Drop any root reproducing a known vertex. Finish with the shoelace determinant in cyclic order and box a number.

hints.hint: When items pass through an intermediate holding spot, model it as a stack: a run is a string of pushes and pops, and the resulting pile read bottom-up is the pop order. Label the items 1..n, write the exact push/pop string that produces the requested arrangement, then price it step by step: factor 1/2 only when both a push and a pop are legal, factor 1 when one side is forced because a stack is empty. Multiply. Two traps: the order is NOT deterministic, and it is NOT uniform over n! -- only stack-permutations occur. Check small cases by hand and confirm probabilities sum to 1. Report exactly one value for the part asked, then stop.

hints.hint: Read these as moment conditions: each a_i is a weight attached to a fixed node i, NOT a coefficient of a polynomial in x. Confusing the two wastes the whole budget. First move: multiply equation k by c_k and add. Then for any test polynomial f(x)=sum c_k x^k using only the exponents actually present (so f(0)=0), you get sum_i a_i f(i) = the same combination of right-hand sides. To isolate one weight, pick f vanishing at 0 and at every other node; that weight then equals the right-hand side over f(its own node). Collapse that product of integer node differences into factorials, fixing the sign by counting negative factors. Verify by re-substituting f. Do not tabulate small cases hoping for a pattern, and do not restart - box the closed form early.

hints.hint: First decide, from the wording alone, whether each given figure is an aggregate or a per-unit amount; if a reading forces an absurd count, drop it at once and never relitigate it. When an unknown count n is pinned down only by integrality, rewrite "each unit's share is a whole number" as "n divides that total": factor the given totals and take their gcd. If the wording still leaves n free, take the largest admissible n, state that choice once, and move on instead of enumerating divisors. Then add the components once, divide by n, and apply a percentage markup as a single multiplication by (1+p); the order of dividing and marking up is irrelevant, so do not redo it both ways. Confirm every per-unit share is an integer, then box the number in the problem's units.

hints.hint: Given p(q(x))=q(p(x)) with unknown coefficients, never expand the composition: degree-9 coefficient matching is what makes solvers run out of room with no answer. First move: posit q = a*p + b, match leading coefficients to pin a via a^3 = a, then substitute u = p(x) (valid, p takes infinitely many values) to collapse everything to the one-variable identity p(a*u + b) = a*p(u) + b. Test each allowed a in one line; discard branches clashing with the given values. The surviving branch makes p antisymmetric about the fixed point m: p(m+t) + p(m-t) is constant. Read each requested value off that symmetry by pairing it with a point you already know, instead of solving for every coefficient. A free coefficient remains: check the answers ignore it, verify the identity numerically at one x, box immediately, never restart.

hints.hint: First move: for the two smallest sizes, write positions 0..N-1 as an explicit list and rewrite the entire list after each stage k=0,1,...,n-1 in order; that is one operation. Reapply it and track the orbit of a single label until it repeats. That cycle length is your candidate order. Then write positions in binary and express the whole operation as one map on bit strings (which bits flip, which rotate), and verify it reproduces both explicit traces. Trap: if traces of different sizes suggest different formulas, your trace is wrong, not the formula piecewise; redo the smallest case letter by letter. Trust the verified bit map over pattern-guessing. Once two sizes agree, stop exploring, never restart the analysis, and box a single closed form in n.
